The BPS is planned and operated within its equipment normal thermal ratings and system voltage limits for

requirements. In addition to satisfactory performance for normal system conditions and for single contingencies, 
the system should be able to withstand some selected “N-2” contingencies when determining stability limitations 
and also extreme (more severe but less probable) disturbances without suffering voltage collapse, cascading, or 
instability.

Evidence describes acceptable voltage at all buses as requiring sufficient reactive resources under normal and contingency operating conditions, and describes contingency/stability analysis (N-1, selected N-2, PV/QV analysis, load flow, or dynamic simulations) as the means to ensure voltage limits and stability, so a normal-voltage observation is at most a normal-condition voltage-limit check, not a stability proof.

What the supplied evidence establishes: reactive power supply is local and voltage-control-related; maintaining acceptable voltage at all buses under normal and contingency operating conditions requires sufficient reactive resources; contingency analysis is conducted for N-1 (and selected N-2) conditions including steady-state and stability requirements; and PV or QV analysis, load flow, and dynamic simulations are listed as study methods.

What is still needed: a defined network model/operating point and contingency set, a voltage-stability assessment (e.g., PV/QV or equivalent) with margins to collapse, and comparison against applicable pre- and post-contingency voltage limits. No such model, operating point, limits, contingency list, or stability study is present here, and no simulation was run, so a stability conclusion is unsupported.

A plant-specific conclusion cannot be drawn from the supplied material; the cited NERC guideline is North American bulk-power-system guidance with region-specific voluntary practices.

excerpt.text:
Contingency Analysis 
The BPS is planned and operated within its equipment normal thermal ratings and system voltage limits for 
conditions where all scheduled elements are in service (Normal condition). Contingency analysis is conducted to 
ensure that the system stays within its emergency thermal ratings and voltage limits immediately after a 
disturbance involving the loss of an element (single contingency or “N-1” condition), but without operator 
intervention. The system should be capable of such performance at all times ,26 including operations during 
minimum and maximum forecasted load conditions. This “N-1” condition applies to both steady state and stability 
requirements. In addition to satisfactory performance for normal system conditions and for single contingencies, 
the system should be able to withstand some selected “N-2” contingencies when determining stability limitations 
and also extreme (more severe but less probable) disturbances without suffering voltage collapse, cascading, or 
instability.

Operating personnel perform studies on a seasonal, monthly, weekly, and day-ahead basis that would identify any 
voltage issues and if necessary would develop remedies. The RC’s EMS continually monitors the system to help 
ensure that all voltages remain within applicable limits for normal conditions. A real-time contingency analysis 
tool is used to help ensure that voltages remain within applicable limits for all single contingencies and select 
multiple-element contingencies. Minimum and maximum v oltage limits for facilities within the region are 
provided to the RC by the TOP. The min/max voltage limits for pre-contingency conditions may be different from 
the limits for post-contingency conditions.
